## Spectator mode and analysis

AI-only games are part of the prototype, because watching them is the only way to see whether trust emerges and to tune the models. The spectator sees everything the engine knows, which no player ever does.

- **God view.** The true map, every treasury, every character's hidden traits and facts, and who knows what.
- **The message trail.** For every message, four versions side by side: what the leader wrote, what the envoy said at the foreign court, what the host answered, and what the envoy reported home. The gaps between them are the game.
- **Who wrote it.** Every message and every decision carries its author: the model that wrote it, a script, a human, or a fallback, a script standing in when a model's call failed. The viewer filters by author, so one model's letter can be found among a season of scripts, and it counts fallbacks aloud, each season saying how many calls fell back and why. A table can set a game to pause when more than a share it chooses fall back, so a broken call cannot quietly turn a model game into a script game. The default is half of a season's model decisions: a starting point, tested and reviewed once model games return (27 October 2026). A decision the budget gives to the script is the script's, not a fallback, and does not count toward the pause ("Minds follow what is at stake").
- **Seat view.** Switch to any power and see exactly what it saw, to judge whether its decisions were reasonable given its information. A model mind's own notes, journal and plan show beside its decisions and spoken words as they stood each season, kept in the record, and after the game in every view (build order item 17+++).
- **Timeline and replay.** Step through turns from the event log, rewind, and replay from the same seed. Everything the narrator writes is stored in the record the first time, so watching a game again never calls a model, unless the game's owner asks for it to be told anew, which keeps the first telling beside the new (build order item 17+++). And a list of threads to watch points the viewer to what is worth watching: a list of the few live stories with the most at stake this season, the narrator's pick from the record, each a click away (follow the person, open the message trail, take the map there), and an optional director camera, off by default, that takes the map to the highest-stakes scene as the season plays out; both choose only what is shown, never what happens, and work the same in replay (build order item 17+++).
- **Signal markers.** Highlight events that count toward the success criteria: sealed tablets, accusations, forgeries, broken promises, coalitions.
- **Speed control.** Run turn by turn while watching, or batch many games unattended and review them afterwards.
- **The map (built in item 2).** A presentation-only makeover, with no change to engine, rules or balance:
  - **Style:** a museum map or archaeological board game, in a Late Bronze Age palette (lapis, carnelian, gold, ochre, clay, bitumen) with light and dark modes for the interface; the map itself keeps its light colours in both, only slightly dimmed in dark mode, as a museum map does (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11c+). Each power is distinct by colour and by pattern or emblem, so it works for colour-blind players. Original period icons: chariots for armies, ships for fleets, a clay tablet or traveller for envoys, oxhide ingots for gold (from item 19, drawn after the period's own relics, each culture in its own idiom: "The look, in time" below).
  - **Geography:** seas, coasts, rivers, mountains, desert and fertility drawn on the map. Terrain is stored as map data matching the siege package, built in item 5.
  - **Readable at a glance:** the whole map fits the screen on phone and desktop, with pinch-zoom; each season's moves, attacks, supports, bounces and captures are shown through the timeline; envoys and gold shipments appear on the road with destination and arrival.
  - **Fog of war as a gradient:** in a seat view, knowledge fades with age, and uncertain information (old sightings, spy reports, rumours) looks uncertain. Each seat sees only the characters it knows about; god view shows everything.
  - **Dates and status:** one date label everywhere (court season and year, with the turn), an ending indicator, and who is asleep in god view.
  - **Measured performance** on a throttled phone, and respect for reduced motion.
- **The map in true geography, and its look in time** (decided 29 October 2026). Haakon: "In my view, the map should in time become a fusion or blend of imperator rome and an ancient museum map of the bronze age world. It should fir the geography the same way imperator has, as it had the best geographic perspective." Two steps:
  - **True geography, now** (build order item 11c). The board takes a true projection of the region, as Imperator: Rome's map does, in place of today's folded board: coasts, rivers, mountains and deserts where they are, each province drawn at its own latitude and longitude, Egypt and Nubia running south along the Nile, the Red Sea drawn, and the deserts at their true size. The Levant is read on a phone by zooming, never by bending the land ("Map on small screens"). Only the drawing changes: distances already come from latitude, longitude and the attested roads. Then (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11c+) provinces take the land's own borders, along the ridges, rivers, desert edges and straits between them rather than straight lines between cities; the lands beyond the game, such as Wilusa, Masa, Ahhiyawa, Keftiu and Libya, are drawn and named as no one's, so the map never ends at a bare edge; and an island that is not a province is no one's.
  - **The look, in time** (build order item 19). A blend of Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age world, in the palette above, drawn on papyrus, the period's own map material, with clay kept for the tablets (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "Maybe it can be papyrus?"). On it: the environment and the seasons (the Nile's flood in Akhet, snow on the Taurus and Zagros passes in Peret, fields turning gold at harvest, drought cracking the land); armies marching as small figures, and battles shown as a clash with their outcome; envoys travelling with their sealed tablets, ships under sail, pirates on the coasts; fog of war as ageing papyrus, older knowledge faded and foxed; and whatever else makes the game better to play or to watch. Everything on it is drawn after the period's own relics, each culture in its own idiom, as close to the originals as looks best and feels most authentic (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "Definetly be fully inspired by these relics, and be in no way afraid of making it too simular. I want what looks best and feels most authentic!"): Egypt's armies after the wooden soldiers of Mesehti's tomb at Asyut, Egyptian spearmen and Nubian archers marching in their companies, and its chariots after Tutankhamun's painted chest; Mitanni's and Assyria's chariots after their cylinder seals; Hatti's and Arzawa's after the marching warrior gods of Yazılıkaya and the Hittite chariots of the Egyptian reliefs; Babylonia's banners after the emblems of the Kassite boundary stones; ships after Tutankhamun's model boats and the Thera flotilla fresco; envoys after the foreign delegations in Meryre II's tomb at Amarna; gold as oxhide ingots; and Alashiya and the Aegean after their clay figurines. So each power's units are told apart by their style as well as their colour; presentation may name a power ("Different data, same rules"). Everything on it comes from the game's own facts, never decoration that could mislead, so the map tells this game's story as it happens (decided 29 October 2026; Haakon: "Agree to everything, expert!"). A map that remembers: battlefields keep a small memorial mark, sacked cities stay in ruins until rebuilt, ravaged fields stay brown until replanted, and lawless land looks wild, so the late map reads as the history of the war. Life from the simulation: towns grow and shrink with their people, caravans move along the trade routes, bands' campfires show where they lurk, refugees stream from a war, siege camps ring a besieged city, and empty granaries show a famine. Every level of what is built shows (Haakon: "I think every investment level infrastructure reaches should reflect on the map. Docks appear. Roads of the wuality appears. Walls. Etc!"): roads drawn by their quality, from track to built road, with their relay stations; harbours from a beach to docks and moorings, with the ships in them; walls by their level, breached where they are breached; water works, wells, cisterns and shafts; granaries and stores by what they hold; mines where they are worked. A seasonal year: the Nile's flood in Akhet, the Levant's hills greening with the winter rains, the Mesopotamian spring flood, summer drying everything brown, storms on the sea in winter and calm water in the sailing season. Each realm's own map: in a seat's view the map is drawn by its own scribes, Egypt's on papyrus with hieratic notes, Babylonia's and Hatti's pressed in clay like the Nippur map tablet, each court in its own medium, while spectators and god view see the papyrus museum map; and knowledge reads the same way, what the seat saw itself in firm ink, a spy's report as a sketch, a rumour as a faint smudge ("Fog of war as a gradient"). Omens in the margin: the darkening omens of the ending appear in the map's border, an eclipse or a strange star, so the end is felt approaching without being told ("Random ending" under Victory). Small scenes at big moments: an envoy's procession arriving at court, a gift caravan with its horses and gold, an ambush on the road as a letter is seized, each brief before the map settles. And fast on a phone: built in layers, the papyrus and the land drawn once, what changes each season over it, and scenes only where something happened. It waits until the features exist, since every item changes what the map must show.
- **Who holds what, and the mood of the land** (decided 31 October 2026, build order item 17++; Haakon: "Agreed with all you said!"). The map's colours show who holds what by oath and office, in three steps of each power's colour: full where the king rules from his own seat, slightly lighter where a governor stands between him and the land, and a faint wash over a vassal's land, so a realm reads at a glance as a firm core, a governed ring and a faint fringe. Each governor's provinces are bounded by a thin inner border, so a man who holds several reads as one bloc, with his name and seat on the province card; vassals keep their own borders and names under their overlord's wash. There is no shade per governor: half a dozen shades of one colour blur on a phone, under the papyrus and for colour-blind players. The colours show the oath and the office, never loyalty, and another realm's governors and vassals only as far as the seat has heard, dated as any news. Loyalty has a view of its own, the mood of the land, one tap away: the king's read of how firmly each province is held, his own and his rivals', in four coarse steps (loyal, uneasy, restless, no word), fading as the read ages and drawn only from what he was told, so it can be wrong ("Loyalty is a ledger"). Travellers' talk gives a region's blurred mood, a governor's report his provinces as honestly as he is honest, and spies, envoys and a census a province at a time. It is not blended into the base colours, since one colour would then mean two things, and a fine gradient would show the hidden ledger as a number in all but name.
- **The main map and its views** (decided 31 October 2026; Haakon: "Agreed to all. Expertly!"). The main map carries as much as it can while staying readable and beautiful (Haakon: "we should try to make the main map as readable and visually appealing we can, so you get most of the information nessecary for you there, while managing not to clutter it too much"). What can be painted is painted, the world as it would look from a hill: snow closing the passes, floods, mud, storms at sea, the land browning in summer, bands' campfires, ruins and siege camps ("The look, in time"), so a king sees how harsh a road is before he opens any view. Only what is out of the ordinary stands out, a closed pass, a famine, a storm, and detail grows as he zooms in, as on Imperator's map. The views are for what cannot be painted, measures, ages and relations, each answering a question a king asks. Nine, one tap each: realms, the default ("Who holds what, and the mood of the land"); the mood of the land; what you know, how old and how sure the seat's news is in each province, from firm ink to a smudge to blank; people, by town and land, with the age of the count, and refugees and migrants as they move; harvest and stores, yields, granaries and hunger; trade, markets, prices as last heard, caravans and routes; roads and seas, days from the capital, road quality, closed passes, crossings, and where bands and pirates were last reported, the main map showing the cause and this view what it costs in days and risk; armies as last reported, each dated, with the seat's own commanders and sieges; and ties, oaths, treaties, marriages and who owes whom, as far as the seat knows. In a seat every view shows only what the seat knows, dated and possibly wrong; in god view the same views show the truth, so the two can be compared. Presentation only: no view changes a rule, and script and model kings read the same facts from the seat view. On a phone, one row of period-styled marks, one tap to switch, a one-line legend, and the main map faint beneath. Each system brings its own view in the item that builds it: realms and the mood of the land come with item 17++, and the visual pass (item 19++) builds the views of every system already in the game.
- **The season plays out, and zoom shapes what you see and hear** (decided 31 October 2026, build order items 17a and 17+++; Haakon: "the player needs to feel the weight of the whole world, or it becomes meaningless to him/her.", then "Agreed, 100% sir!"). A season is not a new picture but a passage of time on the map: the land's season changes beneath the realms, units travel their roads with weight and are drawn as what they are, battles, sieges and the world's hazards play where they happen, paced by meaning so that the great moments can be taken in, with sound on every event; only what the seat knows plays. The engine sends what happened as a stream of events, and the next season is computed while this one plays. Zoom shapes it, as on Imperator's map (Haakon: "If you are zoomed in near a unit in the waves, I want to hear it. And if I zoom in on the map, I like how Imperator makes the state color more and more transparent and you see the ground and effects under more clearly."): zoomed out, the realms' colours are full and the sound is the world's bed and the great moments; zoomed in, the colours thin to a wash and then to borders and banners, the ground, season and figures show through, and what is near the view is heard, louder the nearer. The map's views keep their colours at every zoom. The build order's item 17+++ holds the detail.

The chronicles complete this: after a game, read two nations' biased accounts beside the true record.

**The narrator illuminates; it never steers** (decided 19 October 2026). The game does not know it is telling a story, as Dwarf Fortress does not; its history is only what people did. The narrator's job is to make that history readable, in the spirit of Dwarf Fortress's legends mode, never to shape it, as RimWorld's storytellers choose raids and disasters for drama.

- **Find the thread, don't make it.** The narrator's skill is noticing that the scribe offering a tablet at Hattusa is the man Pharaoh dismissed two years earlier, and that the tablet bears the seal of a court he once served. The engine holds those facts; the narrator connects them. It receives only facts the engine has released and may phrase but never invent them (pillar 6).
- **Its stories are only as good as the record.** If the engine does not record who saw what, who told what to whom, who paid whom and who was where, there is nothing to illuminate. Recording these is part of the design, not a logging detail: "What servants know" serves the narrator as much as the spies.
- **Never a storyteller that steers.** Nothing in the engine nudges events toward a better story: no dramatic timing of catastrophes, no rescue of a losing king, no events because the game has gone quiet. Catastrophes stay seeded and blind to the story.
- **Two kinds of telling.** Each court's chronicle tells its own flattering version, in the Kadesh tone; the true record stands beside them in spectator mode. The gaps between them, like the gaps in the message trail, are part of what is worth reading.

**Legends, read from the record.** The "follow this character" view built with the visual overhaul in item 2 is the first form of a legends mode: one person's life, read from what the engine recorded. Later it can grow into biographies of characters, histories of tablets (who sealed it, who broke it, where copies were shown), and the rise and fall of courts, all of them read from the record and none of them written in advance. When a game ends, the record opens: every hidden fact becomes readable to every seat, who lied, who skimmed, which seals were forged, which go-between was paid to bend what he passed on, and the season the end was drawn for. In a game about deception, that is the moment the table has been waiting for.
